newsitem.title: USA: Small business fears stricter U.S. clean air plan.
newsitem.headline: Small business fears stricter U.S. clean air plan.

text.p: Advocates for small businesses and inner cities on Thursday said the Clinton administration's proposed stricter air quality standards would force jobs from urban areas and hurt small and minority-owned businesses.

"The biggest concern we have in our neighbourhood is crack smoke and gunsmoke because this is what happens when there are no jobs to be had," Ricardo Byrd, executive director of the National Association of Neighbourhoods, said at a news conference.

Byrd and other advocates met earlier on Thursday with Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner to discuss their worries that the EPA's plan to set stricter rules against smog and soot would hurt businesses and urban redevelopment.
The new standards would force expensive pollution controls in urban areas, driving businesses farther into the suburbs and countryside, or overseas, they said.

While the EPA has said the new standards mainly would affect big industries, Harry Alford, president of the National Black Chamber of Commerce, and Peter Homer, president of the National Business Association, said there would be a trickle-down effect on small businesses.
"These unnecessary standards would impose another hurdle for minority-owned businesses, nearly all of which operate in metropolitan areas that would be most affected," Alford said.
But the EPA contends that thousands of lives would be prolonged each year and millions of cases of respiratory problems avoided or eased by meeting the cleaner air standards.
It also has said benefits of reduced time in hospital and missed workdays would more than offset costs to industries of reducing pollution.

"Our goal ultimately is to set a standard that is protective of public health, particularly the health of children. And we believe, too, that any standard that we set will be based on science, and, as history shows, can also be achieved affordably," an EPA official said.
